prompt: In September 1947, what did the operators of the Harvard Mark II tape into their logbook?
options: A moth found trapped in a relay
A cockroach from the card reader
A fly stuck to a vacuum tube
A beetle from the power supply
correctAnswer: A moth found trapped in a relay
explanation: It was found between the points of Relay #70 on Panel F and labeled "First actual case of bug being found." The page is now in the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History.

prompt: The moth found in the Harvard Mark II in 1947 is where the word "bug" for a machine fault comes from.
explanation: Edison was already writing about "bugs" in 1878. The log's joke, "first actual case", only works because the operators knew the slang.

prompt: In the Story of Mel, how did a loop with no test in it still manage to end?
options: Adding one to an address overflowed into the operation code and turned the instruction into a jump
A hardware timer stopped it after a fixed number of drum turns
The operator flipped a sense switch on the console
The drum memory erased the loop after each pass
correctAnswer: Adding one to an address overflowed into the operation code and turned the instruction into a jump
explanation: Mel kept his data at the top of memory, so the carry from the last address spilled into the operation code. It took Ed Nather two weeks to work it out.

prompt: A signed 32-bit count of seconds since 1970 runs out at 03:14:07 UTC on 19 January __________.
explanation: Past +2,147,483,647 the count can roll over to a large negative number, throwing the date back to 13 December 1901. A 64-bit count pushes the limit billions of years away.

prompt: Match each term to what it describes:

pairs.left: First actual case of bug being found
pairs.right: The 1947 note beside the moth in the Mark II log
Drum-memory computer where every instruction named the address of the next
Y2K fix that reads 00 to 50 as the 2000s
A signed 32-bit count of seconds since 1970 running out

explanation: All three stories turn on the limits of a machine: a relay a moth could jam, a drum that set the speed of code, and date fields too small for the future.

prompt: What software fault brought down Ariane 5 on its first flight in 1996?
options: A 64-bit floating-point value was too large to convert to a 16-bit signed integer
Metric and imperial units were mixed up
A clock drifted after running for 100 hours
A cosmic ray flipped a bit in memory
correctAnswer: A 64-bit floating-point value was too large to convert to a 16-bit signed integer
explanation: The value, the horizontal bias BH, came from an alignment routine inherited from Ariane 4 that had no job to do after lift-off. Ariane 5's faster early trajectory made it too big to fit.

prompt: When Ariane 5's active inertial reference system failed, its backup took over and kept the rocket on course for a while.
explanation: The backup ran identical software and had failed 72 milliseconds earlier for the same reason, so duplicating the hardware gave no protection.

prompt: Why did the Patriot battery at Dhahran fail to track the Scud on 25 February 1991?
options: After 100 hours of running, its clock was about a third of a second off, so it looked in the wrong place
Its radar was jammed by Iraqi electronic warfare
It mistook the Scud for a friendly aircraft
It had run out of interceptor missiles
correctAnswer: After 100 hours of running, its clock was about a third of a second off, so it looked in the wrong place
explanation: One tenth has no exact binary form, and the chopped 24-bit value lost a sliver of time with every tick. GAO put the range gate shift at about 687 meters after 100 hours.

prompt: The Vancouver Stock Exchange index sank because after every trade its new value was __________ to three decimal places instead of rounded.
explanation: Truncation always drops value, so the errors never cancel. Corrected over a weekend in November 1983, the index jumped from 524.811 to 1,098.892.

prompt: Match each name to what it describes:

pairs.right: A number too big for a 16-bit integer
One tenth chopped to 24 bits, repeated for 100 hours
Digits dropped, never rounded, after every trade

explanation: None of these failures needed a big mistake: a small number that did not fit, drifted or was trimmed was enough, once it was repeated or trusted at the wrong moment.

prompt: What turned out to trigger the Therac-25 overdoses at the East Texas Cancer Center?
options: Editing the treatment settings quickly
A power cut in the middle of treatment
A worn-out part in the beam
Entering the wrong patient's records
explanation: The hospital physicist had to practice before he could type fast enough to bring up Malfunction 54 at will. The manufacturer's engineer at first could not reproduce it until he was told it had to be done quite rapidly.

prompt: The Therac-20, which shared much of the Therac-25's software, also overdosed patients because of the same flaws.
explanation: The flaws were there, but the Therac-20's hardware safety interlocks kept them from injuring anyone. The Therac-25 replaced many of those interlocks with software checks.

prompt: To stop people faking a "yes", Robert Morris made his worm copy itself anyway one time in __________, even on machines that said they already had a copy.
explanation: Morris underestimated how often each machine would be asked, so the rule produced far more copies than he expected. His was the first conviction under the 1986 Computer Fraud and Abuse Act.

prompt: In Ken Thompson's "Reflections on Trusting Trust", why would reading the compiler's source code not reveal the backdoor?
options: The compiled compiler reinserted the backdoor whenever it compiled itself, so the source could be clean
The backdoor was hidden inside a comment
The source code was encrypted
The backdoor existed only in the login program's source
correctAnswer: The compiled compiler reinserted the backdoor whenever it compiled itself, so the source could be clean
explanation: A compiler can carry knowledge that lives only in its binary, the way it "learns" the code for a newline character. Thompson added that the same trick could hide in an assembler, a loader or even hardware microcode.

prompt: Match each term to its story:

pairs.right: How often the Morris worm copied itself despite a yes
Emergency response center set up after the 1988 worm
The Unix program Thompson's compiler secretly miscompiled

explanation: Each story shows how much can hide inside software: a timing flaw, a growth rule that misfired and a deliberate backdoor that leaves no trace in the source.

prompt: What did Joseph Weizenbaum's secretary ask after typing a few sentences to ELIZA?
options: For him to leave the room
For the computer to be switched off
Whether a person was typing the replies
For a copy of the program
correctAnswer: For him to leave the room
explanation: She knew it was a machine, which is what alarmed him. A historian who searched his MIT papers found mentions of a secretary but never her name.

prompt: Apollo 11's 1202 alarm went off because the guidance computer had more work than time.
explanation: A rendezvous radar problem stole about 13% of the computer's time, so its longest job kept failing to finish. Software restarts cleared the backlog, and Houston called go each time.

prompt: The habit of crediting a computer with understanding and empathy it does not have is called the __________ effect.
explanation: It is named after Weizenbaum's 1966 chatbot, though he never used the term himself. ELIZA worked only by matching key words and reassembling the user's own sentences.

prompt: reCAPTCHA showed two words. How did it know you were human, even though it did not know one of the words?
options: The other word was a known control word, and typing it correctly let you in
It timed how fast you typed
It checked both words against a dictionary
It only showed the test to logged-in users
correctAnswer: The other word was a known control word, and typing it correctly let you in
explanation: The unknown word was shown to several people, and when they agreed, their answer went into the digitized text. By 2014 AI could read the hardest distorted text with 99.8% accuracy, so distorted words alone stopped being a reliable test.

prompt: Match each person to their role:

pairs.right: Wrote ELIZA, then became a critic of AI
Designed the Apollo computer's priority-driven operating system
Led the Software Engineering Division at MIT's Instrumentation Laboratory
Turned CAPTCHAs into a way to digitize old text

explanation: ELIZA fooled people who read too much into it, while Apollo's software and controllers came through because they knew exactly which alarms were safe.
